title: Reading Test 5: Traditional Markets and Local Communities

passage.label: A
passage.text: Traditional markets remain important in many towns even as supermarkets and online delivery services expand. A market is often more than a place to buy food; it can also be a social space where residents meet neighbours, exchange local news, and maintain cultural habits.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Fresh produce is a major attraction. Customers may prefer markets because they can ask sellers where fruit, vegetables, fish, or meat came from. In some places, shoppers also believe that market goods are fresher because they travel through shorter supply chains.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Markets can support small businesses by giving traders a relatively affordable place to sell products. A stall usually requires less investment than a permanent shop. This allows new sellers to test demand before committing to a larger business.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Nevertheless, traditional markets face challenges. Younger shoppers may prefer the convenience of online ordering, and market opening hours may not suit people with long working days. Weather can also affect sales when markets are held outdoors.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Some towns have modernised their markets without removing their local character. Improvements may include clearer signs, covered areas, card payments, and food courts. The aim is not to make markets identical to supermarkets, but to make them easier to use while preserving their community role.
